question: Silicon and germanium are semiconductors. In their pure (intrinsic) state, each atom has:

options.text: One valence electron, which makes them good conductors
Four valence electrons, held in covalent bonds
Three valence electrons, leaving a hole in every bond
Five valence electrons, one of which is always free to move

explanation: Each atom bonds covalently with four neighbours, so at low temperature almost no electrons are free and the pure crystal conducts poorly. Doping with small amounts of three- or five-valence impurities creates the carriers that make devices work.

question: N-type semiconductor material is produced by adding an impurity such as phosphorus or arsenic, which has:

options.text: Four valence electrons, which leaves the material unchanged
Five valence electrons, giving free electrons as majority carriers
Three valence electrons, providing holes as the majority carriers
No valence electrons, which turns the material into an insulator

explanation: A pentavalent ('donor') atom uses four electrons in bonds and donates the fifth as a free carrier. The material is still electrically neutral overall; 'N' refers to the negative charge of its majority carriers.

question: P-type semiconductor material is produced by adding an impurity such as boron or gallium, which has:

options.text: Five valence electrons, creating free electrons as majority carriers
Four valence electrons, so no carriers are added
Six valence electrons, creating both holes and free electrons equally
Three valence electrons, creating holes that act as positive majority carriers

explanation: A trivalent ('acceptor') atom leaves one bond incomplete — a hole. Electrons from neighbouring bonds can move into it, so the hole effectively moves and carries positive charge.

question: As the temperature of a semiconductor rises, its resistance:

options.text: Rises sharply at first and then falls to zero
Rises, in the same way as a metal conductor
Stays constant until it reaches its melting point
Falls, as heat frees more charge carriers

explanation: Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient: heat creates more electron-hole pairs. This is why semiconductor devices can be sensitive to heat, need heat sinks, and can suffer thermal runaway if poorly cooled.

question: A PN junction diode is forward biased when:

options.text: The P-type anode is made positive with respect to the cathode, and it then blocks current
The P-type anode is made positive with respect to the N-type cathode, and it then conducts
No voltage is applied, and it conducts in both directions
The N-type cathode is made positive with respect to the P-type anode, and it then conducts

explanation: Forward bias pushes holes and electrons towards the junction, narrowing the depletion layer until current flows freely. Reverse bias widens the depletion layer and only a tiny leakage current flows (until breakdown).

question: The approximate forward voltage drop across a conducting silicon diode is:

options.text: Zero

explanation: A silicon junction needs about 0.6–0.7 V before it conducts significantly, and that drop stays roughly constant over a wide range of current. Germanium diodes drop about 0.2–0.3 V.

question: In the circuit symbol for a diode, the arrow (triangle) points:

options.text: From anode to cathode, the way conventional current flows
In the direction in which the diode blocks current
From cathode to anode, in the direction of electron flow when it conducts
Towards the positive terminal of the supply in every circuit

explanation: The triangle points in the direction of conventional current when forward biased, towards the bar that marks the cathode. Electrons, being negative, actually move the other way.

question: When a diode is reverse biased, the depletion layer at its junction:

options.text: Stays the same width, and the diode conducts normally
Disappears, and the diode behaves like a resistor
Widens, and only a very small leakage current flows
Narrows, and a large current flows

explanation: Reverse voltage pulls carriers away from the junction, enlarging the region without free carriers. The diode then blocks, apart from a tiny leakage current, until the reverse voltage reaches breakdown.

question: A Zener diode is used mainly as:

options.text: A rectifier for high-current AC supplies, working in forward bias
A switch, turned on by a small gate current
A voltage regulator, working in reverse breakdown
A light source, emitting light when forward biased

explanation: A Zener is designed to break down at a precise reverse voltage without damage. Over a wide range of current its voltage hardly changes, so placed (with a series resistor) across a load it holds the load voltage steady.

question: To act as a voltage regulator, a Zener diode is connected:

options.text: Reverse biased in series with the load, carrying the full load current
Forward biased in series with the load, with no resistor
Reverse biased across the load, with a series current-limiting resistor
Forward biased in parallel with the load, across the supply

explanation: The Zener sets the voltage across the load; the series resistor drops the difference between the supply and the Zener voltage and limits the current, so the diode does not overheat.

question: A light-emitting diode (LED) gives out light when it is:

options.text: Reverse biased beyond its breakdown voltage
Heated above a set temperature
Forward biased and conducting
Exposed to light from another source

explanation: In an LED, electrons and holes recombining at the forward-biased junction release energy as light. LEDs are efficient, long-lived and shock-resistant, which is why they have replaced filament lamps in many aircraft indicators and lights.

question: A photodiode, as used in light-sensing circuits, is normally operated:

options.text: With no bias, as a source of high current for heavy loads
In Zener breakdown, so that its voltage stays constant in all light levels
Forward biased, so that it emits light in proportion to the current
Reverse biased, its leakage current rising with the light falling on it

explanation: Light frees extra electron-hole pairs at the junction, increasing the reverse current in proportion to illumination — useful for automatic display dimming and smoke detectors.

question: A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals called:

options.text: Primary, secondary and core
Emitter, base and collector
Source, drain and gate
Anode, cathode and gate

explanation: In a bipolar transistor, a small current into the base controls a much larger current between collector and emitter. Source, drain and gate belong to a field-effect transistor; anode, cathode and gate to a thyristor.

question: The essential property of a bipolar transistor is that:

options.text: A small base current controls a much larger collector current
It conducts equally in both directions once triggered
Its collector current is independent of its base current
A large base current is needed to pass a small collector current

explanation: Current gain (β or hFE) is the ratio of collector to base current. That is what allows a transistor to amplify a signal, or to act as a switch controlling a load far larger than its own control current.

question: A transistor with a current gain (β) of 100 has a base current of 0.2 mA. The collector current is approximately:

options.text: 2 mA
200 mA
20 mA

question: When a transistor is used as a switch, its two working states are:

options.text: Cut-off (fully off) and saturation (fully on)
Half-wave and full-wave conduction
Forward bias and Zener breakdown
Gate-triggered and holding-current conduction

explanation: As a switch the transistor is driven hard one way or the other: no base current gives cut-off; enough base current gives saturation, where it behaves almost like closed contacts. Operating in between, as an amplifier, it dissipates more heat.

question: An NPN transistor in a common-emitter circuit is switched on by:

options.text: Removing all voltage from its base
Making its base about 0.7 V positive relative to its emitter
Applying a short pulse to its collector
Making its base about 0.7 V negative relative to its emitter

explanation: The base-emitter junction of an NPN transistor is a silicon diode, so it must be forward biased (base positive) by roughly 0.6–0.7 V before base current flows and the transistor conducts. A PNP transistor needs the opposite polarity.

question: A thyristor (silicon controlled rectifier, SCR):

options.text: Latches on when its gate is pulsed, until its current falls below the holding value
Conducts in both directions as soon as any voltage is applied
Blocks all current once its gate has been triggered
Conducts only while its gate current is maintained, just like a transistor

explanation: Once triggered, the thyristor latches on: the gate loses control. In an AC circuit it switches off naturally at the end of each half cycle, so varying the moment of triggering controls the power delivered. A triac does the same in both directions.

question: A field-effect transistor (FET) differs from a bipolar transistor mainly in that it is:

options.text: Current-controlled, needing a large base current to switch on
Voltage-controlled, drawing almost no gate current
A two-terminal device with no control electrode
Able to work only on alternating current

explanation: The gate voltage controls the channel between source and drain through an electric field, with negligible gate current. That makes FETs (and especially MOSFETs) well suited to high-impedance inputs and efficient power switching.

question: A negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor is used in temperature-sensing circuits because:

options.text: Its resistance rises significantly as its temperature rises
It generates a voltage proportional to temperature
It switches abruptly from conducting to non-conducting at a set temperature
Its resistance falls significantly as its temperature rises

explanation: The large, predictable change of resistance with temperature lets a simple circuit (often a bridge) turn temperature into an electrical signal. A thermocouple, by contrast, generates its own small voltage.

question: Semiconductor devices are often mounted on finned metal heat sinks because:

options.text: Heat sinks act as the earth return for the device's current
Semiconductors only conduct when they are cold-soaked
Overheating can lead to thermal runaway and failure
Metal heat sinks increase the forward voltage drop of the junction

explanation: Power devices dissipate heat at the junction. Because their resistance falls as they get hotter, a poorly cooled device can draw more current, heat further and destroy itself. Heat sinks carry the heat away.

question: Many electronic units carry warnings about electrostatic discharge (ESD) because:

options.text: Body static can puncture their very thin internal insulation
Static charge makes the units draw excessive current from the aircraft bus
Static charge changes the doping of N-type material to P-type
Electrostatic discharge magnetises the circuit boards

explanation: Many devices, especially MOS components, have gate insulation so thin that a few hundred volts — far less than you can feel — can damage them. Wrist straps, conductive bags and earthed work surfaces are used when handling such units.
